The dominant religion in Persia before Islam was Zoroastrianism, which dominated the Parthian and Sassanian Empires until the Muslim conquest of Persia between A.D. 633 and 651, after which most Iranian Zoroastrians converted to Islam [d1]. The Sassanian Empire had made Zoroastrianism its official state religion, and when it fell to Muslim Arab invaders in 651 CE, Persian religious practice was suppressed and adherents either converted, fled, or practiced in secret [d8]. Founded by the prophet Zarathustra (Zoroaster) sometime between 1500 and 1000 BC, Zoroastrianism replaced an even older polytheistic Irano-Aryan religion that the ancient Persians had previously practiced — a faith counterpart to the Indo-Aryan religion that became Hinduism [d4]. Before Zoroastrianism, ancient Iranians practiced what is called Iranian paganism or the ancient Iranian religion, worshipping deities such as Ahura Mazda and Mithra, with fire cult practices and sacred liquor sacrifice shared with ancient India [d5][d6]. Zoroastrianism itself is considered one of the world's oldest monotheistic religions, having originated in ancient Persia, and its concepts — including Heaven and Hell, Judgment Day, and angels and demons — influenced Judaism, Christianity, and Islam [d4][d6].
